items.readable_text:
Content:
Recall that a differential equation of the form

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dt} = ky(a-y)]

Content:
is called a logistic growth equation. The positive constant [MATH: a > 0] is the carrying capacity, and [MATH: k > 0] is a constant of proportionality.

Content:
A typical solution curve [MATH: y = y(t)] to this equation is shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/7b26225a7e5506d75b5d629d0df0f96a]

Content:
It can be shown that the general solution to this equation is given by

Content:
[MATH: y(t) = \frac{a}{1+C e^{-ak t}}]
where [MATH: C] is an integration constant.

Content:
Note the following properties of this general solution:

Content:
- Since [MATH: a] and [MATH: k] are both positive, [MATH: e^{-akt}\to0] as [MATH: t\to\infty.] Therefore, [MATH: y(t)\to a] as [MATH: t\to\infty.] In other words, [MATH: y(t)] approaches the carrying capacity as [MATH: t] increases. This agrees with the behavior shown in our diagram.
- Since [MATH: e^{-akt}\to\infty] as [MATH: t\to-\infty,] we have that [MATH: y(t)\to 0] as [MATH: t\to-\infty.] This also agrees with our diagram.

Content:
We can use the general solution of the logistic growth equation to make predictions about a population governed by logistic growth. Let's see how.

sections.normalized_html:
The rate of growth of the panda population [MATH: P(t)] in a particular forest follows the logistic growth model is

[MATH: \dfrac{\mathrm{d} P}{\mathrm{d} t} = 0.001\,25 P(800-P),]

where [MATH: t] is the time, in years, since the beginning of the observations. Find an expression for the panda population after [MATH: t] years, given that there were [MATH: 400] pandas initially.
sections.readable_text:
The rate of growth of the panda population [MATH: P(t)] in a particular forest follows the logistic growth model is

[MATH: \dfrac{\mathrm{d} P}{\mathrm{d} t} = 0.001\,25 P(800-P),]

where [MATH: t] is the time, in years, since the beginning of the observations. Find an expression for the panda population after [MATH: t] years, given that there were [MATH: 400] pandas initially.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
A logistic growth equation has the form

[MATH: \dfrac{\mathrm{d} P}{\mathrm{d} t} = kP(a-P),]

where [MATH: k > 0] is a constant of proportionality, and [MATH: a > P] is the carrying capacity.

The general solution to the logistic growth equation is [MATH: P(t) = \dfrac{a}{1+Ce^{-akt}}.]

In this case, the constant of proportionality is [MATH: k=0.001\,25,] and the carrying capacity is [MATH: a=800.]

Therefore, the general solution to our equation is

[MATH: P(t) = \dfrac{800}{1+Ce^{-(800\cdot 0.001\,25)t}}= \dfrac{800}{1+Ce^{-t}}.]

We now substitute the initial condition [MATH: P(0)=400] and solve for [MATH: C.] We get

[MATH: (800)/(1 + Ce^{− 0})|= 400; (800)/(1 + C)|= 400; (1 + C)/(800)|= (1)/(400); 1 + C|= (800)/(400); C|= 2 − 1; C|= 1.]

Therefore, the panda population is given by

[MATH: P(t)= \dfrac{800}{1+e^{-t}} .]

sections.normalized_html: The growth rate of the hare population [MATH: P(t)] in a particular forest is jointly proportional to the hare population at time [MATH: t,] measured in years, and the difference between the forest's carrying capacity and the hare population. The constant of proportionality is [MATH: 0.000\,01] and the carrying capacity is [MATH: 10\,000.] How many hares will there be in the forest after [MATH: 7] years given that there were [MATH: 2\,500] hares initially? Round your answer to the nearest integer.
sections.readable_text: The growth rate of the hare population [MATH: P(t)] in a particular forest is jointly proportional to the hare population at time [MATH: t,] measured in years, and the difference between the forest's carrying capacity and the hare population. The constant of proportionality is [MATH: 0.000\,01] and the carrying capacity is [MATH: 10\,000.] How many hares will there be in the forest after [MATH: 7] years given that there were [MATH: 2\,500] hares initially? Round your answer to the nearest integer.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Since the hare population's growth rate is jointly proportional to the hare population at time [MATH: t] and the difference between the carrying capacity and the hare population, the hare population follows a logistic growth model.

A logistic growth equation has the form

[MATH: \dfrac{\mathrm{d} P}{\mathrm{d} t} = kP(a-P),]

where [MATH: k > 0] is a constant of proportionality, and [MATH: a > P] is the carrying capacity.

The general solution to the logistic growth equation is [MATH: P(t) = \dfrac{a}{1+Ce^{-akt}}.]

In this case, the constant of proportionality [MATH: k=0.000\,01,] and the carrying capacity is [MATH: a=10\,000.] Therefore, the hare population is given by the equation

[MATH: \frac{\mathrm{d} P}{\mathrm{d} t} = 0.000\,01 P(10\,000-P) .]

The general solution to this equation is

[MATH: P(t) = \dfrac{10\,000}{1+Ce^{-(10\,000\cdot 0.000\,01)t}}= \dfrac{10\,000}{1+Ce^{-0.1t}}.]

We now substitute the initial condition [MATH: P(0)=2\,500] and solve for [MATH: C.] We get

[MATH: P(0)|= 2500; (10000)/(1 + Ce^{− 0.1(0)})|= 2500; (10000)/(1 + C)|= 2500; (1 + C)/(10000)|= (1)/(2500); 1 + C|= (10000)/(2500); 1 + C|= 4; C|= 3.]

So, we have

[MATH: P(t) = \frac{10\,000}{1+3 e^{-0.1 t}}.]

Finally, to find the number of hares in the forest after [MATH: 7] years, we substitute [MATH: t=7] into the expression for [MATH: P(t),] and we get

[MATH: P(7)|= (10000)/(1 + 3e^{− 0.1 ⋅ 7}); ≈ 4016.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Recall that a differential equation of the form

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dt} = ky(a-y)]

Content:
is called a logistic growth equation. The positive constant [MATH: a > 0] is the carrying capacity, and [MATH: k > 0] is a constant of proportionality.

Content:
A typical solution curve [MATH: y = y(t)] to this equation is shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/7b26225a7e5506d75b5d629d0df0f96a]

Content:
It can be shown that the general solution to this equation is given by

Content:
[MATH: y(t) = \frac{a}{1+C e^{-ak t}}]
where [MATH: C] is an integration constant.

Content:
Note the following properties of this general solution:

Content:
- Since [MATH: a] and [MATH: k] are both positive, [MATH: e^{-akt}\to0] as [MATH: t\to\infty.] Therefore, [MATH: y(t)\to a] as [MATH: t\to\infty.] In other words, [MATH: y(t)] approaches the carrying capacity as [MATH: t] increases. This agrees with the behavior shown in our diagram.
- Since [MATH: e^{-akt}\to\infty] as [MATH: t\to-\infty,] we have that [MATH: y(t)\to 0] as [MATH: t\to-\infty.] This also agrees with our diagram.

Content:
We can use the general solution of the logistic growth equation to make predictions about a population governed by logistic growth. Let's see how.

---

Item 2 — Example: Solving a Logistic Growth Initial Value Problem

Example Prompt:
The rate of growth of the panda population [MATH: P(t)] in a particular forest follows the logistic growth model is

[MATH: \dfrac{\mathrm{d} P}{\mathrm{d} t} = 0.001\,25 P(800-P),]

where [MATH: t] is the time, in years, since the beginning of the observations. Find an expression for the panda population after [MATH: t] years, given that there were [MATH: 400] pandas initially.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
A logistic growth equation has the form

[MATH: \dfrac{\mathrm{d} P}{\mathrm{d} t} = kP(a-P),]

where [MATH: k > 0] is a constant of proportionality, and [MATH: a > P] is the carrying capacity.

The general solution to the logistic growth equation is
[MATH: P(t) = \dfrac{a}{1+Ce^{-akt}}.]

In this case, the constant of proportionality is [MATH: k=0.001\,25,] and the carrying capacity is [MATH: a=800.]

Therefore, the general solution to our equation is

[MATH: P(t)
= \dfrac{800}{1+Ce^{-(800\cdot 0.001\,25)t}}= \dfrac{800}{1+Ce^{-t}}.]

We now substitute the initial condition [MATH: P(0)=400] and solve for [MATH: C.] We get

[MATH: (800)/(1 + Ce^{− 0})|= 400; (800)/(1 + C)|= 400; (1 + C)/(800)|= (1)/(400); 1 + C|= (800)/(400); C|= 2 − 1; C|= 1.]

Therefore, the panda population is given by

[MATH: P(t)= \dfrac{800}{1+e^{-t}} .]

Item 5 — Example: Using the Particular Solution of a Logistic Growth Initial Value Problem to Make Predictions

Example Prompt:
The growth rate of the hare population [MATH: P(t)] in a particular forest is jointly proportional to the hare population at time [MATH: t,] measured in years, and the difference between the forest's carrying capacity and the hare population. The constant of proportionality is [MATH: 0.000\,01] and the carrying capacity is [MATH: 10\,000.] How many hares will there be in the forest after [MATH: 7] years given that there were [MATH: 2\,500] hares initially? Round your answer to the nearest integer.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Since the hare population's growth rate is jointly proportional to the hare population at time [MATH: t] and the difference between the carrying capacity and the hare population, the hare population follows a logistic growth model.

A logistic growth equation has the form

[MATH: \dfrac{\mathrm{d} P}{\mathrm{d} t} = kP(a-P),]

where [MATH: k > 0] is a constant of proportionality, and [MATH: a > P] is the carrying capacity.

The general solution to the logistic growth equation is
[MATH: P(t) = \dfrac{a}{1+Ce^{-akt}}.]

In this case, the constant of proportionality [MATH: k=0.000\,01,] and the carrying capacity is [MATH: a=10\,000.] Therefore, the hare population is given by the equation

[MATH: \frac{\mathrm{d} P}{\mathrm{d} t} = 0.000\,01 P(10\,000-P) .]

The general solution to this equation is

[MATH: P(t)
= \dfrac{10\,000}{1+Ce^{-(10\,000\cdot 0.000\,01)t}}= \dfrac{10\,000}{1+Ce^{-0.1t}}.]

We now substitute the initial condition [MATH: P(0)=2\,500] and solve for [MATH: C.] We get

[MATH: P(0)|= 2500; (10000)/(1 + Ce^{− 0.1(0)})|= 2500; (10000)/(1 + C)|= 2500; (1 + C)/(10000)|= (1)/(2500); 1 + C|= (10000)/(2500); 1 + C|= 4; C|= 3.]

So, we have

[MATH: P(t) = \frac{10\,000}{1+3 e^{-0.1 t}}.]

Finally, to find the number of hares in the forest after [MATH: 7] years, we substitute [MATH: t=7] into the expression for [MATH: P(t),] and we get

[MATH: P(7)|= (10000)/(1 + 3e^{− 0.1 ⋅ 7}); ≈ 4016.]
